# Installing Julia and setting up VS Code {#sec-installation}

MiniFEM is written in [Julia](https://julialang.org/). In this book we use
[Visual Studio Code (VS Code)](https://code.visualstudio.com/) as the editor and
development environment.

The installation is operating-system specific only for the first few steps. Once
Julia and VS Code are installed, we will work mainly from the VS Code integrated
terminal and the Julia REPL, so the workflow is essentially the same on Windows,
macOS, and Linux.

::: {.callout-note}
## VSCodium

Readers who do not want to use VS Code can use [VSCodium](https://vscodium.com/)
instead. VSCodium is built from the open-source VS Code codebase without
Microsoft's branding and telemetry.

VSCodium uses the [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/) extension registry rather
than the Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace. For the extension used in this
chapter, the workflow is the same as in VS Code. In the remainder of the
chapter, **VS Code** refers to either VS Code or VSCodium unless stated
otherwise.
:::

## Install Julia

The recommended Julia installation method uses
[Juliaup](https://github.com/JuliaLang/juliaup), Julia's installer and version
manager. Juliaup also takes care of making the `julia` command available from
the command line.

### Windows

Open **Windows Terminal**, **PowerShell**, or **Command Prompt**.

For example, press the Windows key, type `Terminal`, and open **Windows
Terminal**.

Then run:

```console
winget install julia -s msstore
```

Follow the instructions shown by the installer.

If access to the Microsoft Store is disabled on your computer, use one of the
alternative installation methods described in the [official Julia installation
instructions](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/installation/).

### macOS

Open **Terminal**. One quick way is to press `Cmd+Space`, type `Terminal`, and
press Enter.

Then run:

```console
curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh
```

Follow the instructions printed by the installer. When installation is complete,
close and reopen the terminal.

### Linux

Open a terminal from your desktop environment. On many Linux desktops,
`Ctrl+Alt+T` opens one directly.

Then run:

```console
curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh
```

Follow the instructions printed by the installer. When installation is complete,
close and reopen the terminal.

### Check the installation

On any operating system, type:

```console
julia --version
```

A successful installation prints the installed Julia version.

Now start Julia:

```console
julia
```

You should see the Julia prompt:

```text
julia>
```

To leave Julia, type:

```julia
exit()
```

or press `Ctrl+D`.

::: {.callout-important}
## The Julia extension is not Julia

Installing the **Julia extension for VS Code does not install Julia itself**.
Julia must first be installed on the computer using the procedure above.
:::

## Install VS Code

Download and install VS Code from:

<https://code.visualstudio.com/>

Choose the installer for your operating system and use the standard installation
options.

If you prefer VSCodium, install it from:

<https://vscodium.com/>

After installation, start the editor.

## Install the VS Code extension

Open the **Extensions** view by clicking the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar
on the left side of the VS Code window.

Alternatively, open the Command Palette with:

- `Ctrl+Shift+P` on Windows and Linux;
- `Cmd+Shift+P` on macOS;

and run:

```text
View: Show Extensions
```

### Extension used in this project

Install the following extension:

  | Extension | Identifier                 | Purpose                                                                                                                            |
  | --------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | **Julia** | `julialang.language-julia` | Julia language support, integrated REPL, code execution, formatting, navigation, debugging, plots, and other Julia-specific tools. |

## Configure VS Code

VS Code stores user-level configuration in a JSON file called `settings.json`.

Open the Command Palette:

- `Ctrl+Shift+P` on Windows and Linux;
- `Cmd+Shift+P` on macOS.

Then type:

```text
Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)
```

and select that command.

For the Julia workflow used here, the relevant settings are:

```json
{
  "telemetry.telemetryLevel": "off",
  "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
  "julia.enableTelemetry": false,

  "[julia]": {
    "editor.defaultFormatter": "julialang.language-julia",
    "editor.formatOnSave": true
  },

}
```

If your `settings.json` already contains other settings, **do not replace the
whole file**. Add the settings above inside the existing outer braces `{ ... }`
and separate adjacent entries with commas.

The Julia extension uses
[JuliaFormatter.jl](https://github.com/domluna/JuliaFormatter.jl) for
source-code formatting. Therefore, no separate extension or script is needed
merely to format `.jl` files when they are saved.

The MiniFEM project includes its own JuliaFormatter configuration, which is
applied automatically when Julia files are formatted.

## Terminal, shell, and REPL

Three terms are worth distinguishing. A **terminal** is the window or panel
through which we interact with command-line programs. A **shell** is the program
running inside the terminal and interpreting commands. The **Julia
REPL**---short for *read-eval-print loop*---is Julia's interactive environment.

For example, this is a shell command:

```console
julia hello.jl
```

whereas this is Julia code typed at the Julia REPL:

```julia
julia> 2 + 3
5
```

## Open the project from the command line

A convenient workflow is to open VS Code **from the project folder**. This has
an important advantage: VS Code treats that folder as the workspace root, and
terminals and Julia processes started from the workspace naturally begin in the
right location.

::: {.callout-note title="MiniFEM course files"}
The Julia and VS Code installation steps above can be completed without the
MiniFEM files.

At the end of the first class, you will be asked to download the initial course
snapshot, `2026-27/S01-two-springs`, as an archive. After extracting the
archive, you will have a folder named `MiniFEM.jl` containing the project files
used in the following chapters.

From this point onward, commands that refer to the MiniFEM project assume that
you are working with this extracted `MiniFEM.jl` folder.
:::

Open a terminal and move to the MiniFEM project folder. For example:

```console
cd path/to/MiniFEM.jl
```

Check where you are with:

```console
pwd
```

and list the files in the folder with:

```console
ls
```

These commands work directly on macOS and Linux. They also work in PowerShell on
Windows. If you use the older Windows Command Prompt instead, `cd` displays the
current directory and `dir` lists its contents.

Once you are in the project folder, start VS Code with:

```console
code .
```

The dot `.` means **the current directory**, so the command opens the current
project folder as the VS Code workspace.

If you use VSCodium, the corresponding command is normally:

```console
codium .
```

::: {.callout-note}
## If `code` is not available on macOS

On macOS, the `code` command may need to be added to the shell path after VS
Code is installed. Open the Command Palette with `Cmd+Shift+P` and run:

```text
Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH
```

Then close and reopen the terminal. VSCodium provides the corresponding `codium`
command.
:::

The command `code .` opens VS Code in the correct folder; it does **not**
guarantee that the integrated terminal panel will already be visible. If you
need a shell inside VS Code, open:

```text
Terminal > New Terminal
```

The integrated terminal starts at the root of the opened workspace, so `pwd` and
`ls` should show the MiniFEM project folder and its files.

## Starting Julia inside VS Code

There are two related ways to start Julia in VS Code, and they should not be
confused.

### A normal Julia REPL from the terminal

In the VS Code integrated terminal, type:

```console
julia
```

This starts an ordinary Julia REPL in the current folder. Because the terminal
is already in the project folder, relative paths refer naturally to files in
that project.

Create a temporary file named `hello.jl` in the `MiniFEM.jl` project folder
containing:

```julia
println("Hello, MiniFEM!")
```

The instruction

```julia
include("hello.jl")
```

runs `hello.jl` from the current project folder.

### The Julia extension REPL

The Julia extension also manages a Julia REPL that is connected directly to the
editor. This is the REPL used by commands such as **Julia: Execute active File
in REPL** and **Julia: Execute Code in REPL**.

You normally **do not need to start this REPL manually** with:

```text
Julia: Start REPL
```

If a Julia file is open in the editor, click the triangular **Run** button at
the upper-right of the editor and choose or use:

```text
Julia: Execute active File in REPL
```

The Julia extension starts its REPL if necessary and executes the active file
there.

::: {.callout-important}
## The two REPLs are not the same session

Typing `julia` manually in an integrated terminal starts a normal Julia process.
The Julia extension's **Execute ... in REPL** commands use the REPL managed by
the extension. Unless an external REPL is explicitly connected to the extension,
these are separate Julia sessions.

For ordinary MiniFEM work, the simplest editor-based workflow is therefore to
open the project with `code .`, open a `.jl` file, and use the triangular
**Julia: Execute active File in REPL** button. There is usually no need to run
**Julia: Start REPL** first.
:::

## Run Julia code

### From the VS Code editor

Open the `hello.jl` file. With `hello.jl` active, click the triangular button at
the upper-right of the editor:

```text
Julia: Execute active File in REPL
```

This is the most convenient way to run a complete Julia file while developing
interactively.

To execute only the current expression or a selected block of code, use:

```text
Julia: Execute Code in REPL
```

The default shortcut is `Ctrl+Enter`.

### From a Julia REPL

If you started Julia yourself by typing `julia`, run the file with:

```julia
include("hello.jl")
```

### Directly from the command line

You can also run the file without entering an interactive REPL:

```console
julia hello.jl
```

Julia starts, executes the file, and exits. This gives the program a fresh Julia
process.

### Does it work?

You should see:

```text
Hello, MiniFEM!
```

If this output appears, the Julia installation and VS Code setup are ready for
the examples in the following chapters.

You can now delete `hello.jl`. This file is used only to verify the development
environment.

## If VS Code cannot find Julia

With a standard Juliaup installation, the Julia extension should normally find
Julia automatically. Manual configuration should therefore be treated as a
troubleshooting step rather than part of the normal installation.

First open a VS Code terminal and check:

```console
julia --version
```

If this works, restart VS Code, open a `.jl` file, and try the triangular
**Julia: Execute active File in REPL** button again.

If the Julia extension still cannot locate Julia, determine the location of the
executable.

On Windows:

```console
where julia
```

On macOS and Linux:

```console
which julia
```

Then open:

```text
Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)
```

and add the full executable path:

```json
"julia.executablePath": "/full/path/to/julia"
```

On Windows, backslashes must be escaped in JSON. For example:

```json
"julia.executablePath": "C:\\path\\to\\julia.exe"
```

This setting is normally unnecessary and should only be added if automatic
detection fails.
